reference.source: Murray and Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: Characterised by excessive expiratory collapse of the trachea (and often main bronchi) due to weakness of the cartilaginous rings, the posterior membranous wall, or both, producing a crescentic or 'frown-shaped' lumen on dynamic imaging.

Congenital forms associate with prematurity, tracheo-oesophageal fistula/oesophageal atresia, vascular rings and cartilage disorders; acquired forms follow prolonged intubation, tracheostomy, chronic inflammation (relapsing polychondritis), COPD or extrinsic compression.
The cardinal symptom is a harsh, barking or 'seal-like' cough, often with expiratory wheeze, exertional dyspnoea and difficulty clearing secretions leading to recurrent lower respiratory infection.
Symptoms characteristically worsen with any manoeuvre that raises intrathoracic pressure — coughing, forced expiration, crying in infants, or supine posture.

Dynamic (inspiratory-expiratory or cine) CT and awake flexible bronchoscopy with the patient breathing spontaneously are the reference investigations; static end-inspiratory imaging alone frequently misses the diagnosis.
Flow-volume loops may show expiratory flow oscillations or a characteristic notch, but normal spirometry does not exclude the condition.

Distinguish primary cartilage/membranous weakness (tracheomalacia) from dynamic excessive collapse driven by an over-compliant posterior membrane (excessive dynamic airway collapse), as management emphasis differs.
Continuous positive airway pressure can act as a pneumatic stent, relieving symptoms and guiding suitability for surgical stabilisation such as posterior tracheobronchopexy.
reference.pathophysiology: Tracheomalacia results from structural weakness of the tracheal wall so that it cannot maintain patency against the transmural pressure swings of respiration. Weakness may lie in deficient or soft cartilaginous rings (reducing the normal cartilage-to-membrane ratio) or in an excessively lax, redundant posterior membranous wall. During expiration and cough, positive intrathoracic pressure exceeds the airway's structural resistance, so the intrathoracic trachea collapses inward, dynamically narrowing the lumen; the extrathoracic trachea, by contrast, tends to collapse on inspiration. This flow limitation impairs secretion clearance, promotes air trapping and turbulent flow, and predisposes to mucus retention and recurrent infection. Congenital disease reflects intrinsic cartilage immaturity or maldevelopment (often with associated foregut or vascular anomalies), whereas acquired disease reflects cartilage destruction or degeneration from pressure necrosis, chronic inflammation, or long-standing extrinsic compression.
additionalDifferentials: asthma with poorly reversible airflow obstruction
vocal cord dysfunction / inducible laryngeal obstruction
extrinsic tracheal compression by mediastinal mass or vascular ring
excessive dynamic airway collapse from an over-compliant membranous wall
additionalInvestigations: dynamic inspiratory-expiratory (cine) CT of the central airways
awake flexible bronchoscopy during spontaneous and forced breathing
pulmonary function testing with flow-volume loop analysis
trial of continuous positive airway pressure as a diagnostic-therapeutic stent
echocardiography or CT angiography where vascular ring or compression is suspected
evaluation for relapsing polychondritis where cartilage inflammation is suspected
contrast oesophagram if tracheo-oesophageal fistula or vascular ring is possible
redFlags: recurrent 'dying spells', cyanotic or apparent life-threatening events in an infant
acute respiratory distress with inability to clear secretions
recurrent or non-resolving lower respiratory tract infection
syncope or near-syncope precipitated by cough (cough syncope)
rapidly progressive dyspnoea suggesting associated systemic cartilage disease
reference.prognosis: Congenital tracheomalacia frequently improves as the airway cartilage matures over the first one to two years of life, whereas acquired and syndromic forms tend to be persistent and may progress; severe or diffuse disease carries appreciable morbidity but can respond well to positive-pressure support or surgical stabilisation in selected patients.
pitfalls: Relying on static end-inspiratory imaging or a single bronchoscopic snapshot, which can miss dynamic expiratory collapse.
Misdiagnosing the barking cough and wheeze as refractory asthma and escalating bronchodilators or steroids without benefit.
Overlooking a treatable underlying cause such as a vascular ring, mediastinal mass or relapsing polychondritis.
Placing airway stents indiscriminately, as they carry substantial complications including granulation, migration and infection.
Failing to recognise associated gastro-oesophageal reflux or aspiration that perpetuates airway inflammation.
